name: Spinal decompression therapy

lead: Non-surgical spinal decompression uses a computerized table to gently stretch the spine, mainly marketed for disc herniation and nerve pain.
Small trials report pain and disc outcomes in lumbar patients. None examine posture or appearance.

paras: Segmental distraction is said to reduce pressure on discs and nerve roots, and some studies measure changes in disc height or herniation size.
The reviewed sources do not detail adverse effects. A 2007 review questioned whether the literature supported the efficacy claims in advertising.

lead: Non-surgical spinal decompression therapy is a table-based form of traction, usually computerized, offered by chiropractors and physical therapists for disc herniation and radiculopathy. The term spinal decompression also covers surgeries such as microdiscectomy and laminectomy that relieve pressure on nerves [1].
In looksmaxxing and posture circles it is mentioned for disc and spine concerns. It is a medical treatment for back pain and is not documented as an appearance procedure.
Small randomized trials report pain and disc outcomes in lumbar patients [2][3][4], while a 2007 review questioned whether the literature supported efficacy claims made in advertising [5].

paras: Spinal decompression in general means relief of pressure on the spinal cord or nerve roots. Surgical forms include microdiscectomy and laminectomy; non-surgical forms include traction and physiotherapy [1]. The non-surgical devices use computerized feedback to deliver segmental distraction to the spine [4].
No studies found on spinal decompression therapy for appearance outcomes. Trials in lumbar disc patients exist.

A double-blind randomized trial of 20 patients reported on herniation resorption and disc height [6]. A study of 30 patients compared a decompression device with general traction for pain, disability and straight leg raising [2], and another compared manual therapy with decompression on pain and disc height [3]. A 2022 randomized trial examined adding decompression to routine physical therapy in lumbar radiculopathy [4], and other trials examined subacute herniations [7] and combination with core exercises [8]. Wikipedia reports a 2022 meta-analysis finding mechanical traction better than conventional physiotherapy in the short term but not in all studies longer than six months [1]. A 2007 review asked whether the scientific literature supported claims made in advertising [5].
